A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLMFP research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material. Some new reporting inconsistencies create local ambiguities but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on nine planning tasks, baseline comparisons, component ablations, task-specific prompting experiments, and runtime and cost results.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original Sokoban results, success-rate evaluations, baseline controls, resource comparisons and paraphrase testing.

M1.justification: The five-stage pipeline, six-field JSON representation, Z3 code generation, retry and self-assessment procedures remain unchanged. The MILP adaptation already appears in v1. New notation and revised examples clarify the existing method.

E1.justification: The original nine tasks remain. v2 adds a small Sokoban benchmark involving grid navigation and box pushing, plus mathematical-description Coffee and paraphrased-description Blocksworld scenarios. These extend coverage within the existing planning scope.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add Code-SMT using both GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet across the original nine tasks. This introduces a substantive solver-matched comparator alongside the retained Direct, CoT, unrestricted Code and o1-preview baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds feasibility-based success rates, explicit-optimality baseline re-evaluations, formal mathematical inputs for Coffee, a 15-query Sokoban protocol and a 50-query Blocksworld paraphrase test. Original temperature and iteration limits remain unchanged. The paraphrase experiment's model is ambiguous: its prose and caption specify Claude 3.5 Sonnet, while Table 15 headers specify GPT-4o.

E4.justification: New analyses test explicit optimality instructions, sensitivity to paraphrasing, and whether formal Coffee inputs overcome direct-planning failures. v2 also adds baseline error analysis and Sokoban failure analysis. The original component ablations, iteration curves, task-specific examples and LLMFP failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting; average runtime and cost tables do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing accuracy entries in Tables 1–4 remain, but Code-SMT becomes the strongest Claude multi-constraint baseline at 62.4%, narrowing LLMFP's reported margin from 36.5 to 18.3 percentage points. v2 adds success, Sokoban, prompting-control, paraphrase and comparative resource results. Movie component timings also change: Formulator 31.9 to 21.2 seconds and Solver 15.6 to 9.9 seconds, without a stated protocol revision.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds explicit optimization formulations and a benchmark-complexity treatment involving max-flow, independent-set and TSP arguments, plus Blocksworld hardness attribution. These introduce substantive mathematical claims absent from v1, although the arguments are sketches rather than complete proofs. Section 3's additional notation mainly restates the existing pipeline.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the general-purpose zero-shot planning contribution, novelty positioning and headline 83.7%/86.8% optimal-rate claims. The additional evaluations support existing claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations of formalization versus optimization ability, feasibility versus optimality, resource tradeoffs, paraphrase robustness and Sokoban scaling limitations. It retains the principal ambiguity and solver-dependence limitations. The specific explanation for Warehouse's improved no-Definer ablation is removed, although its underlying API-overwriting failure remains documented.

D1.justification: v1 promises future release of full task prompts; v2 states they are available through its newly supplied project page. v2 also discloses baseline output formatters. Existing prompt templates and solver limits remain, while the seven Coffee query-group sample counts are omitted from Section 4.4.

R1.justification: v2 adds Raman et al. (2024), Manas et al. (2024), and Gupta and Nau (1992), including a brief comparison with temporal-logic planning. The main research positioning remains unchanged. Consolidating duplicate Kambhampati references does not remove that prior work.

P1.justification: v2 tightens related-work and experimental prose, expands the Overview and Formulator explanations, and introduces consistent symbolic notation. It adds acknowledgments and reorganizes appendix subsections while retaining the main section sequence and much of the original wording.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation expands substantially with new success-rate, efficiency, Sokoban and control tables, plus Code-SMT rows in Tables 1–2. Figure 2 replaces four isolated variable examples with paired Coffee and Blocksworld formulations. Existing iteration plots and most appendix figures are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: Solver-matched comparisons and explicit-optimality controls address weaknesses in v1's evaluation, while success-rate and resource results make the advantages more assessable. These gains are tempered by new reporting ambiguities, particularly Table 15's conflicting model labels, and inadequately justified complexity arguments: Appendix A.1's TSP claims are not reconciled with the scheduling and fixed-order routing definitions in Figures 7–8. The net improvement is useful but qualified.
